title: The Enochian Alphabet
subtitle: 21 Letters of the Angelical Script
primarySource: Sloane MS 3189 (Liber Loagaeth), Dee's working papers
scholarlyAuthority: Donald Laycock, The Complete Enochian Dictionary (1978/1994)

fontInfo.note: Enochian fonts use ASCII range, mapping letters to the codepoints of their English equivalents. Several freely available fonts exist (Enochian, Enochian Writing, etc.).

scriptOriginNote.text: The Enochian script shares graphical similarities with a script attributed to the prophet Enoch that appeared in the Voarchadumia Contra Alchimiam of Johannes Pantheus (1550), a copy of which Dee is known to have owned.

orthographyNote.text: Enochian orthography closely follows Early Modern English orthography, including soft/hard c and g, and the digraphs ch, ph, sh, and th.

dee.description: Long [ɑː] when stressed, short [a] (the TRAP vowel) when unstressed
dee.englishApprox: Like 'ah' when stressed, like 'a' in 'cat' when unstressed

goldenDawn.description: Pronounced as its name 'Un' or as the long vowel [ɑː]

historicalNote.text: First letter received in the alphabet transmission of March 26, 1583. Dee mapped it to the English letter A.

dee.description: [b]; silent after m when before another consonant or word-final
dee.englishApprox: Like English 'b'; silent in clusters like 'mb' before a consonant

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter B. The silent-b-after-m rule mirrors Elizabethan English pronunciation conventions.

scholarlyNotes.observation: The cluster rules for B follow English phonotactics, not those of any Semitic or other ancient language.

dee.description: [k] before a, o, u (hard c); [s] before e, i and in consonant clusters (soft c). Dee marks soft c with 's' in his pronunciation notes.
dee.englishApprox: Like 'k' in 'cat', or 's' in 'city' — same rules as English

goldenDawn.description: Varies by context; no single syllabic rendering standardized

modern.description: Pronounced as the English letter c with standard soft/hard rules

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter C. The soft/hard c distinction follows English orthographic conventions exactly.

scholarlyNotes.observation: The soft/hard c rule is English, not Latin or Semitic. This is one of the strongest arguments for English as the language's phonological substrate.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'd'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter D. Straightforward phonological mapping with no special rules.

dee.englishApprox: Like 'ay' in 'say' when stressed, like 'e' in 'bet' when unstressed

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter E. Dee marked stressed vowels in most words, allowing reconstruction of the stressed/unstressed distinction.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'f'

goldenDawn.description: Pronounced [ɛf] as in the English letter name

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter F. Also appears as part of the digraph 'ph' which equals [f], following English orthography.

dee.description: [ɡ] before a, o, u (hard g); [dʒ] before e, i, word-finally, after d, and in consonant clusters. Dee writes 'dg' for soft g.
dee.englishApprox: Like 'g' in 'go' (hard), or 'g' in 'gem' (soft) — Dee notes 'zorge' rhymes with 'George'

goldenDawn.description: Varies by context; no single syllabic rendering

modern.description: Pronounced with English soft/hard g rules

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter G. Dee's pronunciation note that 'zorge' rhymes with 'George' is one of the clearest phonetic instructions in the manuscripts.

scholarlyNotes.observation: The 'zorge/George' rhyme is a key piece of evidence for reconstructing Elizabethan pronunciation of Enochian.

dee.description: [h] in most positions; silent in the digraphs ch [k/tʃ], ph [f], sh [ʃ], th [θ]; silent after a vowel (in which case the vowel is lengthened)
dee.englishApprox: Like English 'h'; silent in 'ch', 'ph', 'sh', 'th'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter H. The digraph system (ch, ph, sh, th) exactly mirrors English orthographic conventions, not Latin or Greek.

scholarlyNotes.observation: Dee indicated in some places that 'ch' is to be pronounced as [k], following the same ambiguity found in English loanwords from Greek.

dee.description: [j] word-initially before a vowel (consonantal); as a vowel: [iː] when stressed, [ɪ] when unstressed. Y is treated as a variant of I.
dee.englishApprox: Like 'y' at start of syllable before vowel, like 'ee' when stressed, like 'i' in 'bit' when unstressed

historicalNote.text: Mapped to both I and Y. The I/Y equivalence reflects Elizabethan orthographic practice. Dee did not distinguish between them as separate letters.
historicalNote.source: Laycock (2001); Dee's alphabet table in Sloane MS 3189

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'l'

goldenDawn.description: No standardized syllabic rendering; varies by practitioner

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter L. Note that J and K are absent from the Enochian alphabet — Dee treated them as unnecessary, following Latin orthographic tradition.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'm'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter M.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'n'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter N. The Golden Dawn's alternative pronunciation [nuː] derives from Westcott's method of inserting Hebrew vowel sounds after consonants.

scholarlyNotes.observation: Westcott's method allows each letter to be pronounced either as its English name or as the first consonant and vowel of its Hebrew name — e.g., N may be [ɛn] or [nuː] (from nun).

dee.description: [oː] when stressed, [ɒ] when unstressed; the digraph 'oo' is [uː]
dee.englishApprox: Like 'oh' when stressed, like 'o' in 'hot' when unstressed; 'oo' like 'oo' in 'moon'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter O. The 'oo' = [uː] digraph follows English orthographic convention.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'p'; 'ph' like 'f'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter P. The 'ph' digraph follows English/Greek orthographic tradition.

dee.englishApprox: Like 'qu' in 'queen'; the word 'q' (meaning 'thy') sounds like 'kwa'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter Q. The standalone word 'q' [kwɑː] meaning 'thy' is one of the shortest attested Enochian words.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'r' (Elizabethan r was likely a tap or trill, not the modern approximant)

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter R. Note that Elizabethan English R was likely a different sound from the modern English approximant — closer to a tap [ɾ] or trill [r].

dee.description: [s] or [z] as natural in English context; the digraph 'sh' is [ʃ]
dee.englishApprox: Like English 's' or 'z'; 'sh' like 'sh' in 'ship'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter S. The s/z alternation and the 'sh' digraph follow English phonological patterns.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 't'; 'th' like 'th' in 'thin'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter T. The 'th' digraph for [θ] is a distinctly English orthographic convention.

dee.description: [uː] when stressed, [ʊ] when unstressed; [juː] in initial position; [v] or [w] before a vowel
dee.englishApprox: Like 'oo' in 'moon' stressed, like 'u' in 'put' unstressed; like 'v' or 'w' before vowels

modern.description: Pronounced as English u or v depending on position

historicalNote.text: Dee treated U and V as positional variants of the same letter, which was standard Elizabethan practice. This letter therefore maps to both modern English U and V. W is omitted entirely from the Enochian alphabet.

scholarlyNotes.observation: The U/V merger and the absence of J, K, W are consistent with Latin-influenced English orthography of the 1580s, not with an independent linguistic tradition.

dee.englishApprox: Like English 'x' in 'box'

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter X.

dee.description: [z]; rarely [zɒd], the 16th-century English name of the letter Z
dee.englishApprox: Like English 'z'; sometimes pronounced 'zod' as a standalone syllable

historicalNote.text: Mapped to the English letter Z. The pronunciation [zɒd] reflects the 16th-century English name for the letter Z (compare French 'zède').

scholarlyNotes.observation: The [zɒd] pronunciation as a syllable is characteristic of Elizabethan English — by the 18th century, 'zed' had become standard in British English.

omittedLetters.note: Three modern English letters are absent from the Enochian alphabet: J, K, and W. Dee treated I/Y as a single letter (Gon) and U/V as a single letter (Van), following standard Elizabethan orthographic practice.

_dataStatus.verificationNotes: All letter names, English equivalents, and phonological values cross-checked against Laycock's table and Leitch's analysis. IPA values from Laycock's phonological reconstruction. Golden Dawn syllabic readings from Laycock's report of Westcott's method. Badge assignments follow CLAUDE.md §Badge Discipline.
